title: Fed Hikes Into Sticky Inflation as the Global Long End Sells Off
content:
The window's defining story was a Fed that pivoted back to tightening against still-sticky inflation. On 16 September the FOMC raised its target range by 25bp to **3.75%-4.00%**, its first hike in over three years, following a firm August payrolls print, with the dot plot flagging more to come and headline inflation stuck near **3.4%**.

The sharper move came at the long end, where a global rout drove the US 10-year from below 5% towards **5.28%** by 2 October — the highest since 2007 — in a classic **bear-steepening** blamed on sticky inflation, resilient growth and swelling deficits.

Higher long rates lifted discount rates across equities, credit and housing, firmed the dollar and left markets braced for something to break. Auction demand and the Fed's next signal remained the swing factors into the fourth quarter.

title: AI Megacap Concentration Collides With Rising Discount Rates
content:
Equity leadership stayed tethered to a handful of AI megacaps, leaving benchmarks hostage to single names just as climbing yields pressured the richest valuations. The ten largest S&P 500 members swelled to a record **41%** of the index, exceeding even the dot-com peak.

Across the four weeks the bubble debate intensified, with strategists warning that soaring hyperscaler capex and stretched multiples sat uneasily with a 10-year marching towards 5%. The S&P 500 still held within roughly **2%** of its record near **7,640** even after the Fed hike, but **narrow breadth** left it exposed to any AI stumble.

The set-up sharpened the central Q4 question of whether AI earnings can justify valuations as discount rates climb. With megacaps steering direction, their durability became the market's key vulnerability.

title: Gold Holds Record Territory as a Debasement and Safe-Haven Hedge
content:
Gold's entrenchment in record territory remained a defining cross-asset trend. Bullion held above **$4,000** throughout, trading a volatile path into the **$4,400s** before easing back towards **$4,200** by month-end.

The resilience was striking because it persisted despite a firm dollar and surging real yields — normally stiff headwinds for a non-yielding asset. Steady central-bank buying and robust investor demand instead pointed to a structural bid and a **debasement hedge** against heavy deficits, sticky inflation and geopolitical risk.

With both bonds and the richest equities wobbling, gold offered diversification few other assets could match. Its ability to hold firm against high real rates made its momentum a closely watched gauge of underlying investor anxiety.

title: Middle East Supply Risk Keeps a Premium Embedded in Crude
content:
A persistent Middle East **supply shock** ran through the window, with constrained flows through the Strait of Hormuz — the world's most important oil chokepoint — keeping a risk premium embedded in crude even as regional production slowly recovered.

Prices stayed elevated but two-way. Brent briefly spiked above **$109** early in the period on fresh attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure, before easing back towards **$100** as alternative export routes and gradually rising output capped the upside.

The shock mattered because elevated energy fed directly into inflation prints and hawkish central-bank rhetoric, reinforcing the higher-for-longer rates story. A renewed Hormuz disruption stayed the key upside tail for prices — and the main downside tail for global risk assets.
